title: Reduction dimension and exact orthogonality
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field] with a nontrivial real-valued multiplicative nonarchimedean absolute value. A norm $N$ on a $K$-vector space means $N(x)=0$ exactly for $x=0$, $N(x+y)\le\max(N(x),N(y))$, and $N(ax)=|a|N(x)$. Put $\widetilde K=\{|a|\le1\}/\{|a|<1\}$ and $\widetilde V=\{N(v)\le1\}/\{N(v)<1\}$. If $V$ has finite dimension and an orthogonal basis (a basis $v_i$ with $N(\sum a_iv_i)=\max_i|a_i|N(v_i)$), and $N(V\setminus\{0\})\subset |K^\times|$, then $\dim_{\widetilde K}\widetilde V=\dim_K V$. For every finite field extension $L/K$ with spectral norm $s$ [lem-trf-incomplete-spectral-algebra-norm], $s(z^m)=s(z)^m$ for $m\ge1$, its reduction $\widetilde L=\{s\le1\}/\{s<1\}$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional reduced $\widetilde K$-algebra, and $\dim_{\widetilde K}\widetilde L\le[L:K]$. Moreover, equality $\dim_{\widetilde K}\widetilde L=[L:K]$ holds if and only if $L$ admits a basis $v_i$ satisfying $s(v_i)=1$ and $s(\sum a_iv_i)=\max_i|a_i|$. Neither completeness nor separability is assumed.

proof.text: Write $K^\circ=\{a:|a|\le1\}$ and $K^{\circ\circ}=\{a:|a|<1\}$. The absolute-value inequalities make the first a ring and the second a proper ideal. Every element outside the ideal has norm $1$, so its inverse lies in $K^\circ$; consequently $\widetilde K$ is a field. For a normed vector space $(W,N)$, the sets $W^\circ=\{N\le1\}$ and $W^{\circ\circ}=\{N<1\}$ are $K^\circ$-modules, and $K^{\circ\circ}W^\circ\subset W^{\circ\circ}$ by scalar homogeneity. Thus $W^\circ/W^{\circ\circ}$ is a $\widetilde K$-vector space: changing a scalar or vector representative changes its product by a vector of norm $<1$. In particular a class represented by $w\in W^\circ$ is nonzero exactly when $N(w)=1$.

proof.text: For the first assertion, let $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ be the given orthogonal basis. Choose $c_i\in K^\times$ with $|c_i|=N(v_i)$, using the value-group hypothesis, and put $e_i=c_i^{-1}v_i$. Then $N(\sum a_ie_i)=\max_i|a_i|$. It follows that $\sum a_ie_i\in V^\circ$ exactly when all $a_i\in K^\circ$, and that it belongs to $V^{\circ\circ}$ exactly when all $a_i\in K^{\circ\circ}$. Reducing coefficients therefore gives a bijective linear map $\widetilde K^n\to\widetilde V$, with basis the classes of the $e_i$. By [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], both dimensions are $n$. If $V=0$, the empty basis gives $\widetilde V=0$ and both dimensions are $0$.

proof.text: Now let $L/K$ be finite and $s=s_{L/K}$. The algebra norm properties in [lem-trf-incomplete-spectral-algebra-norm] show that $L^\circ=\{s\le1\}$ is a commutative ring, that $L^{\circ\circ}=\{s<1\}$ is an ideal, and that $s(a\cdot1)=|a|$. Hence the quotient is a $\widetilde K$-algebra and the scalar map is injective: $a\in K^\circ$ maps to zero exactly when $|a|<1$. Since $s(1)=1$, its unit is nonzero. A finite field extension is algebraic, so [lem-trf-algebraic-spectral-norm-powers] gives $s(z^m)=s(z)^m$ without completeness or separability. If $\bar z^m=0$ for some $m\ge1$, then $s(z)^m=s(z^m)<1$, whence $s(z)<1$ and $\bar z=0$. Thus $\widetilde L$ is reduced.

proof.text: For a finite independent family $\bar w_1,\ldots,\bar w_r$ in $\widetilde L$, choose lifts $w_i\in L^\circ$; each has $s(w_i)=1$. Given coefficients $a_i\in K$ not all zero, choose $j$ with $|a_j|=M=\max_i|a_i|>0$. The vector $y=\sum_i(a_i/a_j)w_i$ has $s(y)\le1$. If $s(y)<1$, reduction would give $\sum_i\overline{a_i/a_j}\,\bar w_i=0$, contradicting independence since the $j$th coefficient is $1$. Therefore $s(y)=1$ and $s(\sum_i a_iw_i)=M$. For zero coefficients both sides are zero. In particular every such lifted family is $K$-linearly independent.

proof.text: Put $n=[L:K]$. Applying [lem-weil-independent-family-card-le-dimension] to the lifted family of Step 4 gives $r\le n$ for every finite independent family in $\widetilde L$. Start with the empty family in $\widetilde L$ and append a vector outside its span whenever the span is proper. The appended family is independent: in a relation, a nonzero last coefficient would express the new vector in the old span, and a zero last coefficient reduces to old independence. This must terminate at or before $n$ vectors, since otherwise the first $n+1$ vectors contradict the bound. The resulting independent spanning family is a finite basis. Its size is $\dim_{\widetilde K}\widetilde L$ by [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], so the reduction is finite-dimensional and its dimension is at most $n$.

proof.text: Assume equality in the dimension bound. A basis of $\widetilde L$ has $n$ elements by [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. Lift it as in Step 4 to $w_1,\ldots,w_n$. These are independent over $K$. If their span in $L$ were proper, appending a vector outside that span would give $n+1$ independent vectors (the relation argument in Step 5), contradicting [lem-weil-independent-family-card-le-dimension] for the $n$-dimensional space $L$. They therefore form a $K$-basis. Step 4 gives $s(w_i)=1$ and exactly the required norm formula for every coefficient family. Conversely, a basis with the stated formula is orthogonal and all nonzero values on $L$ belong to $|K^\times|$, because a nonzero finite coefficient family attains a nonzero maximum. Step 2 then gives equality of the dimensions.
